title: Native programs and exit codes
summary: Call git, tar, robocopy or any .exe from PowerShell correctly: the call operator, arguments, $LASTEXITCODE versus $?, Start-Process, and making a script fail when a program fails.

steps.title: Running programs from PowerShell
body: Any program on the PATH runs by name: `git status`, `tar -czf a.tgz dir`, `robocopy src dst /MIR`. Its output comes
back as **strings**, one per line, so you can pipe it (`git branch | Select-String feature`) or capture it
(`$branch = git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`).
- **`&`** (the call operator) runs a command whose name is in a variable or has spaces:
`& 'C:\Program Files\7-Zip\7z.exe' a backup.7z .\data`, or `& $tool @args`.
- **Arguments** are passed one per item: a variable with spaces is one argument, an array is several
(`tar -czf $archive @folders`). Since PowerShell 7.3 quoting rules for native programs are predictable
(`$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing`); in 5.1, embedded quotes were famously broken.
- **stderr**: in PowerShell 7, a program's stderr lines are shown but are **not** errors. `2>$null` drops them,
`2>&1` merges them into the output.
**The exit code is the only reliable signal**, and PowerShell keeps it in **`$LASTEXITCODE`**:
```powershell
git fetch origin
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "git fetch failed with exit code $LASTEXITCODE" }
`$?` is `$true`/`$false` for the last command of any kind; `$LASTEXITCODE` is the number from the last **program**.
Note that `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` does **not** stop on a failing program by default. Since PowerShell 7.4,
`$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true` makes a non-zero exit code a real error.

steps.prompt: A script starts with `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`. Then `tar -czf backup.tgz ./missing` fails with exit code 2. What happens next?
options: The script carries on with the next line: `'Stop'` only applies to PowerShell errors unless `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` is `$true`
The script stops with an error
steps.explain: Programs report failure through their exit code, which PowerShell stores in `$LASTEXITCODE` without treating it as an error. Check it after every program that matters, or turn on the 7.4+ preference variable.

steps.title: backup complete (it was not)
prompt: `~/scripts/backup.ps1` archives folders with `tar`. Last night a folder was missing, tar failed, and the script still
said `backup complete` and exited 0. Reproduce it:
Fix the script so a failing `tar` makes it **exit non-zero** without printing `backup complete`. A normal run must
still create the archive and exit 0.

checks.name: a failing tar fails the script
checks.cmd: out=$(pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/backup.ps1 -Folder ~/app/missing 2>&1); rc=$?; echo "$out"; echo "exit $rc"; test $rc -ne 0 && ! echo "$out" | grep -q 'backup complete'
checks.fail: With a missing folder the script must exit non-zero and not say `backup complete`.

checks.name: a normal run still archives both folders
checks.cmd: rm -f ~/backup/*; pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/backup.ps1 >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?; f=$(ls ~/backup/*.tar.gz | head -n1); test $rc = 0 && tar -tzf "$f" | grep -q customers.csv && tar -tzf "$f" | grep -q app.json
checks.fail: A normal run should exit 0 and write an archive in `~/backup` containing `app.json` and `customers.csv`.

hints: After the `tar` line, `$LASTEXITCODE` holds tar's exit code (2 here).
Add `if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "tar failed with exit code $LASTEXITCODE" }` right after the tar line. An uncaught `throw` in `pwsh -File` exits with 1.
solution: (Get-Content ~/scripts/backup.ps1 -Raw).Replace('tar -czf $archive @Folder', "tar -czf `$archive @Folder`nif (`$LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw `"tar failed with exit code `$LASTEXITCODE`" }") | Set-Content ~/scripts/backup.ps1 -NoNewline
explain: Learn the exit codes of the programs you script: `robocopy` returns **0 to 7 for success** (8 and above are
failures), `msiexec` returns 3010 for "success, reboot needed", `grep` returns 1 for "no match". A blanket
`-ne 0` is wrong for those, so check the documented ranges.

steps.title: Start-Process, and when not to use it
body: Calling a program directly (`git ...`, `& $exe ...`) is the default: it waits, its output is yours, and
`$LASTEXITCODE` is set. **`Start-Process`** is for the other cases:
```powershell
$p = Start-Process msiexec.exe -ArgumentList '/i', 'agent.msi', '/qn', '/norestart' -Wait -PassThru
$p.ExitCode                                                 # 0, or 3010 = reboot needed
Start-Process pwsh -Verb RunAs                               # Windows: a new elevated window (UAC prompt)
Start-Process notepad.exe -ArgumentList 'report.txt'        # start a GUI program and do not wait
- Without `-Wait` it returns at once; without `-PassThru` you get no process object (and no exit code).
- Its output does **not** come back to your pipeline; use `-RedirectStandardOutput file.txt` if you need it.
- `-NoNewWindow` keeps a console program in the current window (Windows).
So: `git`, `tar`, `kubectl`, `az`: call directly. Installers, elevation, GUI apps, other users: `Start-Process`.

steps.title: A git helper: every repo at a glance
prompt: You have a dozen repos checked out and want one command that says which branch each is on and whether it has
- for each **Git repository** directly under `-Path` (sorted by name), output an object with `Repo` (the folder
name), `Branch` and `Changes` (the number of lines in `git status --porcelain`);
- folders that are not repositories are **skipped silently** (no git error on screen).

checks.name: one object per repo with branch and changes
checks.fail: Expected `billing main 0`, `portal feature/sso 2` and `reports release/2026.11 3`, in that order.

checks.name: non-repositories are skipped silently
checks.cmd: pwsh -NoProfile -c '& ~/scripts/Get-RepoStatus.ps1 -Path ~/repos' 2>&1 | grep -Ei 'fatal|not a git|not-a-repo' && exit 1; exit 0
checks.fail: `~/repos/not-a-repo` should produce neither an object nor a `fatal: not a git repository` message. Send git's stderr to `$null` and check `$LASTEXITCODE`.

hints: `git -C <folder> rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` prints the branch, and exits with 128 in a folder that is not a repository.
`$changes = @(git -C $dir.FullName status --porcelain)`: the `@()` makes zero lines an empty array with `.Count` 0.

`foreach ($dir in Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $Path -Directory | Sort-Object Name) { $branch = git -C $dir.FullName rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>$null; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { continue }; ... [pscustomobject]@{ Repo = $dir.Name; Branch = $branch; Changes = $changes.Count } }`
explain: Wrapping a CLI in a function that returns objects is one of the highest-value things PowerShell does: now
`Where-Object Changes -gt 0`, `Export-Csv` and `Sort-Object Branch` all work on git's answers. Use the CLI's
machine-readable output (`--porcelain`, `--format`, `-o json`), never the human one, which changes between versions.

steps.prompt: On Linux, what does this print?
code: "`$? is $? and the exit code is $LASTEXITCODE"
steps.answer: $? is False and the exit code is 2
steps.explain: GNU `ls` exits with 2 for a missing file; `2>$null` only hides its message. `$?` is `$false` because the last program failed. In a double-quoted string, the backtick keeps the first `$?` literal.
